title: Chapter 104 — The Fossil Whale
paragraphs: With his mighty bulk, the whale offers a most congenial theme on which to enlarge, amplify, and generally expand. Even if you wanted to, you could not compress him. By rights he should only be treated in imperial folio, the largest size of book. Not to count over again his furlongs from spout-hole to tail and the yards he measures around the waist — only think of the gigantic coils of his intestines, where they lie in him like great cables and hawsers coiled away on the underground orlop-deck of a ship of the line.

Since I have undertaken to manhandle this Leviathan, I must prove myself omnisciently exhaustive in the enterprise — not overlooking the tiniest seminal germs of his blood, and spinning him out to the last coil of his bowels. Having already described him in most of his present habitat and anatomical peculiarities, it now remains to magnify him from an archaeological, fossiliferous, and antediluvian point of view. Applied to any other creature than the Leviathan — to an ant or a flea — such portly terms might fairly be judged unjustifiably grandiloquent. But when Leviathan is the text, the case is different. I am glad to stagger into this undertaking under the weightiest words in the dictionary. And let it be said here that whenever it has been convenient to consult one in the course of these dissertations, I have always used a huge quarto edition of Johnson, bought expressly for that purpose, because that famous lexicographer's uncommon personal bulk made him better fitted to compile a dictionary for a whale author like me.

We often hear of writers who rise and swell along with their subject, even when it may seem an ordinary one. So what about me, writing about this Leviathan? Without my meaning it, my handwriting grows into poster capitals. Give me a condor's quill! Give me Vesuvius' crater for an inkwell! Friends, hold my arms! For the mere act of writing down my thoughts about this Leviathan wears me out and makes me faint, they reach out so widely and take in so much, as if they would include the whole circle of the sciences, and all the generations of whales and men and mastodons, past, present and to come, along with all the turning panoramas of empire on earth and across the whole universe, not leaving out its suburbs. That is how much a large, generous theme can magnify a writer! We swell to its size. To produce a mighty book, you must choose a mighty theme. No great and lasting book can ever be written about the flea, though plenty of people have tried.

Before taking up the subject of fossil whales, I present my credentials as a geologist by stating that in my odd moments I have been a stonemason, and also a great digger of ditches, canals and wells, wine-vaults, cellars, and cisterns of all sorts. Likewise, by way of preliminary, I want to remind the reader that while in the earlier geological strata are found the fossils of monsters now almost completely extinct, the later relics discovered in what are called the Tertiary formations seem to be connecting links, or at any rate intervening links, between those creatures from before recorded time and the ones whose remote descendants are said to have entered the Ark. All the fossil whales discovered so far belong to the Tertiary period, which is the last one before the surface formations. And though none of them exactly matches any known species of the present time, they are still similar enough to them in general respects to justify their being ranked as Cetacean fossils.

Detached, broken fossils of pre-Adamite whales — fragments of their bones and skeletons — have been found at various intervals within the past thirty years at the base of the Alps, in Lombardy, in France, in England, in Scotland, and in the states of Louisiana, Mississippi, and Alabama. Among the more curious of these remains is part of a skull which in 1779 was dug up in the Rue Dauphine in Paris, a short street opening almost directly on the palace of the Tuileries; and bones dug up while excavating the great docks of Antwerp in Napoleon's time. Cuvier pronounced these fragments to have belonged to some utterly unknown Leviathanic species.

But by far the most wonderful of all Cetacean remains was the nearly complete, enormous skeleton of an extinct monster found in 1842 on Judge Creagh's plantation in Alabama. The awestruck, credulous slaves who lived nearby took it for the bones of one of the fallen angels. The Alabama doctors declared it a huge reptile and gave it the name Basilosaurus. But when some sample bones were taken across the sea to Owen, the English anatomist, this supposed reptile turned out to be a whale, though of a species now gone. That is a telling example of the fact this book has repeated again and again: the whale's skeleton gives very little clue to the shape of his body when fully clothed in flesh. So Owen renamed the monster Zeuglodon, and in his paper read before the London Geological Society he declared it, in substance, one of the most extraordinary creatures that the changes of the globe have wiped out of existence.

When I stand among these mighty Leviathan skeletons, skulls, tusks, jaws, ribs, and vertebrae — all showing partial resemblances to the existing breeds of sea-monsters, but at the same time bearing similar likenesses to the annihilated Leviathans from before recorded time, their incalculable elders — I am carried back as if by a flood to that wondrous period before time itself can be said to have begun; for time began with man. Here Saturn's gray chaos rolls over me, and I catch dim, shuddering glimpses of those polar eternities when wedged bastions of ice pressed hard on what are now the Tropics, and in all the 25,000 miles of this world's circumference not a hand's breadth of habitable land was visible. Then the whole world was the whale's; and, king of creation, he left his wake along the present lines of the Andes and the Himalayas. Who can show a pedigree like Leviathan? Ahab's harpoon had shed older blood than Pharaoh's. Methuselah seems a schoolboy. I look around to shake hands with Shem. I am horror-struck at this existence of the unspeakable terrors of the whale — older than Moses, without a source — terrors which, having been before all time, must of necessity go on existing after all human ages are over.

But this Leviathan has not only left his pre-Adamite traces in the stereotype plates of nature, and bequeathed his ancient bust to limestone and marl; on Egyptian tablets too, so old that they seem almost fossils themselves, we find the unmistakable print of his fin. In a room of the great temple of Denderah, some fifty years ago, there was discovered on the granite ceiling a sculptured and painted planisphere, a map of the heavens, crowded with centaurs, griffins, and dolphins, like the grotesque figures on the celestial globes of the moderns. Gliding among them, old Leviathan swam as in days of old; he was there, swimming in that planisphere, centuries before Solomon was in his cradle.
Nor must I leave out another strange testimony to the antiquity of the whale, in his own bony, after-the-Flood reality, as recorded by the venerable John Leo, the old Barbary traveler.

"Not far from the seaside, they have a Temple, the rafters and beams of which are made of whale-bones; for whales of a monstrous size are often cast up dead on that shore. The common people imagine that by a secret power bestowed by God on the Temple, no whale can pass it without immediate death. But the truth of the matter is that on either side of the Temple there are rocks that shoot two miles into the sea and wound the whales when they come upon them. They keep a whale's rib of an incredible length as a miracle, which, lying on the ground with its convex side uppermost, makes an arch whose top cannot be reached by a man on a camel's back. This rib (says John Leo) is said to have lain there a hundred years before I saw it. Their historians affirm that a prophet who prophesied of Mahomet came from this Temple, and some do not hesitate to assert that the Prophet Jonas was cast out by the whale at the base of the Temple."
In this African Temple of the Whale I leave you, reader; and if you are a Nantucketer and a whaleman, you will silently worship there.
